chunks: "Ground probe points matter because the probe's ground connection is part of the circuit I'm measuring, and a long one gives wrong answers.
A normal oscilloscope probe has a ground clip lead about 15 centimetres long, and that's roughly 100 to 200 nanohenries. The probe tip has about 10 picofarads of capacitance.
Together they form a series LC circuit: with 150 nanohenries and 10 picofarads the resonant frequency is about 130 megahertz.
A fast edge, like a switching node or a clock, excites it, and I see ringing and overshoot on the screen that isn't really on the board.
The same loop also picks up magnetic fields from nearby inductors and switch nodes, so a ripple measurement shows spikes that aren't real.
So I put a ground pad or loop right next to every test point I care about, ideally with a via to the plane, and I use the probe's tip-and-barrel with a short spring ground.
With 15 millimetres of ground path the resonance moves to about 400 megahertz and the overshoot falls from about 50 percent to about 7.
Ground points also help production test and bring-up: fixtures and bed-of-nails need ground contacts, and you want one near each rail so you can measure ripple and noise quickly.
And I make sure the points are on the right ground, so I'm not measuring a floating or noisy section."
